newsitem.title: UK: Hume in initiative to defuse N.Ireland march.
newsitem.headline: Hume in initiative to defuse N.Ireland march.

text.p: Nobel peace prize nominee John Hume on Sunday announced an initiative to defuse tension building over a Protestant Orange Order parade in July which last year sparked the worst civil unrest in Northern Ireland for decades.

Hume, leader of the Social Democratic and Labour Party (SDLP), said that he and the Grand Master of the Orange Order, Robert Saulters, would hold talks with the residents of Garvaghy Road, the flashpoint for last year's violence.

It was the first time that the Orange Order, whose Protestant members want Northern Ireland to stay British, had agreed to negotiate with Garvaghy Road residents -- Catholic Irish nationalists who identify with Dublin.
"This is a breakthrough and I look forward to all sides coming together. I hope all participants will approach this in a positive frame of mind," Hume said in a statement.
Last July police banned the annual parade from the Protestant church at Drumcree down the Garvaghy Road area of the town of Portadown, but reversed the ban after province-wide rioting by Protestants.
The U-turn ignited Catholic anger instead and paralysed the province for a few days as barricades were thrown across highways and police attacked with petrol bombs and stones.

Hume's initative was announced as a tense standoff developed in the village of Dunloy, 50 miles (80 km) north of Belfast where a march by a Protestant order, the Apprentice Boys, was stopped by a protest from Catholic village residents.
Hundreds of Apprentice Boy marchers were prevented by 70 police jeeps and hundreds of police, including riot squads, from approaching the village, which is predominantly Catholic.
They had intended to walk to a small church in the village but police banned the parade and then axed an alternative route to an Orange Order hall because of local opposition.

There were a few minor scuffles and stones were thrown at police before the marchers dispersed, vowing to return in the near future and complete a parade they say they have been carrying out for 47 years.
"This is not the end of this. We feel deeply hurt. We do intend to walk to our place of worship again," the Apprentice Boys' leader, John Finlay, told reporters.

The standoff highlighted the potential for confrontation in Northern Ireland during the so-called marching season, when Protestants parade their pro-British loyalty in marches whose origins date back hundreds of years.
Catholics, a 40 percent minority in Northern Ireland, say such parades celebrate centuries-old Protestant victories over Catholics and are triumphalist and intimidatory.
But Protestants say they are a birthright and a harmless tradition which celebrates their British identity and Protestant faith and are not intended to offend anyone.
